item.title: Texas AI Data Centers Spark Political Pushback and Energy Concerns
item.description:
Texas AI Data Centers Spark Political Pushback and Energy Concerns

Texas is experiencing a surge of AI‑focused data center construction that has ignited political battles, tax‑exemption controversy, and rising energy‑use concerns.

📈 Growth of AI Data Centers

  • “Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas.”
  • “The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry.”
  • “In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs.”
  • “As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years.”

⚖️ Political Backlash

  • “There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park.”
  • “Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says.”
  • “The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments.”
  • “And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers.”
  • “The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction.”
  • “Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state.”
  • “A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found.”
  • “That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents.”
  • “Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma.”
  • “Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project.”
  • “That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups.”

💰 Financial Impact

  • “The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015.”
  • “But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years.”

⚡ Energy and Environmental Concerns

  • “Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand.”
  • “Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found.”
  • “Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems.”
  • “Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates.”

🗳️ Electoral Stakes

  • “After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state.”
  • “The state’s high‑profile Senate race is no less of a nail‑biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico.”

📊 Public Opinion Poll

Party / Group Opposition %
Overall Texans 57
Republicans 43
Democrats 75
Independents 54

#Texas #DataCenters #AIInfrastructure #EnergyPolicy

Source: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers

item.title: US fossil fuel infrastructure surge as renewables slow and AI data center demand rises
item.description:
US fossil fuel infrastructure surge as renewables slow and AI data center demand rises

🔍 Overview

The new report from the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy shows the United States is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down. Data centers are demanding more energy, and the Trump administration is making sure fossil fuels meet the moment.

⚙️ Key details

  • “The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.”
  • Electricity demand is climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid.
  • Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 % of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 % by the second quarter of 2026.
  • If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 % of the development pipeline by the end of the decade.
  • Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 GW by 2030, a 45 % jump from construction plans six months earlier.
  • Renewable projects are being cancelled at a faster rate than fossil projects (4.9 % vs. 2.9 %).
  • Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown.

📊 Energy mix and costs

  • The U.S. still generates 60 % of its electricity from fossil fuels, but wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024.
  • Solar was the fastest‑growing source of new electricity generation in 2024, accounting for 81 % of added capacity.
  • New utility‑scale solar and wind farms cost $68–$69 per MWh on average, compared with $90 per MWh for new combined‑cycle natural gas plants.
  • Fossil fuels are subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran.

💡 Why it matters

  • “The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.
  • If all gas projects in the development pipeline are completed, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades.
  • Gas and coal plants emit air pollutants and greenhouse gases, leading to higher health costs.
  • Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.
  • The administration’s policies have sought to hobble wind and solar while promoting fossil fuels, including issuing stop‑work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives.
  • The forecasted surge in AI data‑center energy demand is a key driver behind the renewed focus on fossil‑fuel‑intensive power generation.

The report was published last week and analyzes data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

#EnergyPolicy #FossilFuels #Renewables #AI

Source: The fossil fuel comeback is here

item.title: US House to Vote on Bipartisan Bill Protecting Households from Data Center Power Costs
item.description:
US House to Vote on Bipartisan Bill Protecting Households from Data Center Power Costs

The US House of Representatives is expected to vote on the bipartisan ‘Ratepayer Protection Act’ this Wednesday. The legislation aims to prevent the soaring costs associated with data center expansion and power needs from being passed on to average household electricity bills.

🔍 Overview

Introduced by Representative Kathy Castor (D-FL) and Representative Gabe Evans (R-CO), the bill seeks to ensure that large data centers pay their fair share of the costs for expanding the electricity grid. The proposal comes as government officials face pressure to manage the increasing energy demands of the AI industry while protecting consumer affordability and grid reliability.

🧩 How it works

  • Cost Allocation: State utility regulators would be required to consider whether large electricity users should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them.
  • Capacity Threshold: The proposed rules would require new data centers using at least 20 megawatts to cover the additional power infrastructure costs they create.
  • Rate Reductions: Regulators would have the authority to charge large data centers extra to help lower the bills of other utility customers.
  • State Authority: The bill would give states more freedom to impose conditions, such as requiring data centers to secure new power supplies or placing limits on their electricity usage.

⚙️ Key details

The following reactions and perspectives have been reported regarding the proposed legislation:

Entity or Individual Position Perspective
Hakeem Jeffries House Democratic Leader Called the proposal an ‘appropriate step forward’ but noted ‘more clearly needs to be done.’
Allison Clements Former FERC member Described the bill as a ‘modest step in the right direction’ that signals congressional alignment on protecting customers.
Craig Sundstrom Amazon Energy Policy Director Stated the bill ‘could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster.’
Ari Peskoe Harvard Electricity Law Initiative Highlighted that no other industry’s electricity usage has captured so much political attention.
Technology Industry Official (Via Axios) Described certain provisions as an ‘unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment’ for a single industry.

💡 Why it matters

While data centers have existed for decades, the growth of AI has significantly increased the demand for new power plants and grid upgrades. This shift has raised concerns regarding higher costs for households. The bipartisan support for the bill arrives ahead of the November midterm elections, highlighting the political priority of grid reliability and consumer costs. While Amazon suggests the bill could accelerate infrastructure investment, the Data Center Coalition is currently reviewing the legislation. Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta did not respond to requests for comment.

#DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #ArtificialIntelligence #Legislation

Source: US moves to stop AI data centres from pushing up household electricity bills. Here’s what could change for Americans

item.title: Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs
item.description:
Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs

Congress is scrambling to address voter concerns over the impact of AI data centers on residential electricity rates as lawmakers debate new legislative measures. With the data center industry rapidly expanding, regional utilities are building tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in new infrastructure, raising questions about how much of these costs will be passed on to everyday utility customers.

⚖️ Legislative Initiatives

Several data center and AI-related bills are moving through Congress. The primary competing measures include:

Bill Name Sponsor / Promoter Key Provisions & Status
Ratepayer Protection Act Sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted Would have state utilities consider holding “large-load” customers responsible for increased costs. Passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support; opposed by Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.
GRID Savings Act Authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich; promoted by Sen. Chuck Schumer Aimed at protecting ratepayers; described by Schumer as having “more teeth” than the Ratepayer Protection Act because the Ratepayer Protection Act’s protections are voluntary.

⚙️ Rising Infrastructure and Utility Costs

The rapid growth of data centers has significantly impacted regional energy grids and wholesale electricity costs:

  • Overall Ratepayer Impact: PJM, a regional transmission organization serving 13 states and the District of Columbia (including Northern Virginia), has an Independent Market Monitor estimating that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers approximately $29 billion over roughly the past two years.
  • State-Level Costs: Maryland customers pay an estimated $168 to $216 more per year on electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom.
  • Infrastructure Demands: Utilities are constructing new power lines, substations, and other grid-connecting infrastructure. Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, notes, “We’re talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities.”
  • Cost Recovery: Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Virginia, stated, “We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers.”

🧩 Challenges in Determining Consumer Impact

Calculating the precise cost passed on to residential ratepayers is difficult due to several variables and a lack of transparency:

  • Local Variables: According to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland, consumer impact depends on utilities’ power-purchasing contracts, retail rates, regulatory decisions, the scale of upgrades, and how utilities share accounting.
  • Lack of Transparency: Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative, states that a “single, clean number” for nationwide data center costs is impossible because much of the data regarding what data centers pay is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
  • Prevalence of NDAs: A study by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved, or proposed data centers.

💡 Political Ramifications

The issue of data center growth and energy costs has also entered political campaigns. Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted is currently in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted’s past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue.

#AIdatacenters #EnergyPolicy #RatepayerProtection #GridInfrastructure

Source: Data centers

item.title: US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices
item.description:
US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices

The United States is pressing European governments to release a portion of their strategic diesel reserves in order to ease price pressures and address supply disruptions.

🔍 Overview

  • The American Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright, proposed a coordinated plan to release diesel from European strategic reserves.
  • The proposal targets 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days.
  • This amount is more than one‑third of the roughly 315 million barrels that EU countries held in reserve in June.
  • US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also supported the measure in a post on X.
  • President Donald Trump indicated he could ask Europe to tap their diesel reserves during a visit to Texas.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Release target: 120 million barrels of diesel.
  • Time frame: 180 days.
  • Share of EU reserves: > 33 % of the 315 million barrels reported in June.
  • Winter timing: The minister said, “It is time to bring the diesel stocks to market in a coordinated manner,” as winter approaches.

🗣️ Political Statements

  • Chris Wright told Fox News, “Europe can also contribute to improving the situation.”
  • Scott Bessent wrote on X, “Our European partners should accelerate the implementation of their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”
  • President Donald Trump said in Texas, “We could do that. They have diesel,” indicating he could ask Europe to release reserves.
  • On Thursday, Trump’s tone was described as less forceful.

💡 Why it matters

  • Releasing diesel could help lower fuel prices in the United States and Europe.
  • Coordinated market entry aims to stabilize supply ahead of the winter heating season.
  • The request reflects ongoing tensions over President Trump’s earlier threat to impose an export ban on US diesel.
  • European participation would demonstrate trans‑Atlantic cooperation on energy security.

#Diesel #EnergyPolicy #USEuropeRelations

Source: US government calls on Europe to release part of diesel reserves to lower prices

item.title: California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures
item.description:
California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed seven bills on Monday that aim to increase transparency around data centers’ electricity and water consumption.

🔍 Overview

  • Data centers are expanding across the U.S., prompting protests over potential strain on power grids and local water supplies.
  • The new California legislation seeks to give communities better data and more say on how data centers impact electricity bills and water supply.

🧩 Legislative Details

Bill Requirement
SB 886, SB 1168, AB 2383 Direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup grid‑connection costs
AB 1577 Requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption
AB 2619, AB 2469 Require water‑use disclosures; AB 2469 also makes operators cover infrastructure‑upgrade costs
SB 887 Removes categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act, ensuring data centers undergo environmental review

⚙️ Why it matters

  • Without clear data, scientists have found it “extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
  • The disclosure rules begin next year but still won’t provide a full picture of consumption.
  • Two possible outcomes are outlined: (1) ballooning electricity demand could lead to costly new infrastructure that may be overbuilt if AI demand falls, passing costs to other consumers; (2) spreading fixed grid‑maintenance costs across more customers could lower electricity rates, but this depends on data centers contributing to distribution‑system costs rather than only connecting to high‑voltage transmission.
  • Water‑use data remain opaque; water providers have refused to share usage figures, and current disclosures only apply when seeking permits or business licenses, leaving year‑to‑year usage unclear.

📊 Perspectives

  • “I’m happy [AB 1577] passed,” Specht said, noting the difficulty in researching state offers.
  • “I wouldn’t say definitively that data centers have increased the cost [of electricity],” he added, acknowledging the lack of numbers to demonstrate either increase or potential savings.
  • As data centers’ power needs grow, monitoring their energy and water consumption becomes increasingly important.

#California #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #WaterUse

Source: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that

item.title: California Governor Signs Laws Regulating AI Data Center Energy and Water Use
item.description:
California Governor Signs Laws Regulating AI Data Center Energy and Water Use

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of seven bills designed to regulate the utility consumption of AI data centers and prevent them from passing costs onto residents.

⚙️ Key details

The new legislation mandates several operational requirements for data centers:

Requirement Description
Rate Classification The California Public Utilities Commission must introduce a new rate classification for data centers.
Infrastructure Costs Data centers are required to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.
Transparency Proposed data centers must disclose estimated water use, energy efficiency, and drought planning to local governments.
Approval Process Facilities must meet specific energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements to qualify for a streamlined approval process.

💡 Why it matters

Governor Newsom stated that these laws aim to ensure that those profiting from data centers do not do so at the expense of residents. He noted that the regulations address community concerns regarding electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution. Additionally, the Governor signed a separate executive order last week to accelerate the creation of an AI “kill switch.”

#California #AI #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #Regulation

Source: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
